description.summary: Aka Manto ('Red Cloak') is a Japanese urban legend about a masked, red-cloaked spirit who haunts public and school toilets and asks the occupant to choose between red or blue toilet paper (or red or blue cloak). Either choice ends in death; only refusal lets the victim escape.
description.full: Aka Manto (赤マント, 'Red Cloak'), also known as Red Cape, Red Vest, or in some regional variants Aoi Manto ('Blue Cloak'), is a long-standing Japanese urban legend told in schoolyards from at least the 1930s. According to the most common form of the tale, a masked male spirit wearing a flowing red cloak appears to people sitting on the toilet in a public or school bathroom — typically the last stall, late at night — and asks whether they want red paper or blue paper. Choosing red causes the victim to be slashed or flayed until their blood soaks through their clothes, producing the 'red cloak'; choosing blue causes them to be strangled or drained of blood until their skin turns blue. Naming any other colour brings a worse death (often being dragged into the floor or 'underworld'). Survival requires either ignoring the spirit or refusing both options. Variant forms swap the toilet paper for cloaks or capes, or substitute the Kainade legend in which a hairy yokai's coloured arm reaches up from inside the toilet. According to folklorist Matthew Meyer, accounts circulate from as early as the 1930s; one tradition places the legend's origin in an Osaka elementary school around 1935, with the legend reaching Tokyo within a year or two and spreading to Kitakyushu and Japanese-administered Korea by 1940. The historic word 'manto' originally referred to a sleeveless kimono-style jacket and only later came to mean a Western-style cloak, which has produced generational variation in retellings. Aka Manto sits within a network of Japanese school-toilet legends including Hanako-san, the Akaname, Teke Teke, and Kuchisake-onna.

etymology.origin: Japanese; combination of 赤 (aka, 'red') and マント (manto, originally a sleeveless kimono jacket, later a Western-style cloak or cape).
etymology.first_use: School-yard rumour from at least the 1930s; the term 'manto' shifts in meaning across the 20th century, producing both 'red coat / vest' and 'red cloak / cape' descriptions of the entity.

related_phenomena.name: Hanako-san
related_phenomena.description: Female schoolgirl ghost said to haunt school toilets, especially the third stall

related_phenomena.name: Kuchisake-onna
related_phenomena.description: Slit-mouthed woman urban legend with a similar choice-based killing structure

related_phenomena.name: Teke Teke
related_phenomena.description: Legless schoolyard ghost from Japanese urban legend

features.description: A flowing red cloak, cape, or coat — the defining attribute of the entity.
A white mask covering the face; in some accounts the face beneath is described as supernaturally beautiful.
Almost always presented as a male spirit, though some variants leave the gender ambiguous.

physical.morphology: A humanoid spirit form, the visible features of which are entirely determined by costume (red cloak, white mask).

abilities.description: Appears in occupied public or school toilet stalls, usually the last stall, late at night.
Offers the victim a binary choice (red or blue paper / cloak); either answer is lethal in a colour-coded way (slashing for red, strangulation/exsanguination for blue).
Naming a colour other than red or blue brings being dragged through the floor to the underworld in many tellings.
Can be escaped by ignoring or explicitly refusing both options.

patterns: Targets people alone in toilet stalls late at night
Frames its attack as an apparently neutral choice
Punishes deviation from its expected script

range.description: Originally a Japanese school-yard legend; widely retold across Japan and exported through pop culture to East Asia, North America, and beyond.

first_recorded.source: Schoolyard rumour reported by Matthew Meyer and other Japanese-folklore writers

peak_activity_periods.description: Pre-war and wartime spread from Osaka through Tokyo and Kitakyushu to Japanese-administered Korea
Resurgence of the legend with the wider Japanese 'school horror' boom
Global spread through anime, video games, and films

origins.cultural_roots: Japanese school-yard storytelling of the early Showa era (1920s–30s); shaped by anxieties about the modern public bathroom, schoolyard rumour, and the era's red-cloaked criminal scares.
origins.earliest_accounts: Reports as early as the 1930s; one tradition fixes the origin around 1935 in an Osaka elementary school.
origins.folklore_connections: Closely linked to other school-toilet legends (Hanako-san), to choice-based killing legends (Kuchisake-onna), and to bathroom yokai (Akaname).

timeline.event: Aka Manto reportedly originates in an Osaka elementary school, according to a tradition recorded by Matthew Meyer
timeline.significance: Earliest dating of the legend in the secondary literature
timeline.source: Wikipedia: Aka Manto, citing Matthew Meyer

timeline.event: The legend reaches Kitakyushu and Japanese-administered Korea
Aka Manto appears as the antagonist of episode 2 of the anime Ghost Stories (Gakkō no Kaidan)
Eric Grundhauser publishes 'Aka Manto Is the Bathroom Ghost That Wants You to Choose Wisely' in Atlas Obscura
Indie horror studio Chilla's Art releases the Aka Manto video game
timeline.significance: Modern interactive retelling of the legend

timeline.event: Squid Game premieres on Netflix; director Hwang Dong-hyuk later confirms its red/blue card colour scheme is a nod to Aka Manto
timeline.significance: Mass-audience exposure to the legend's choice motif

history.modern_era: Aka Manto remains a living urban legend told in Japanese schools and a recurring reference in international horror media, video games, and anime.

documentary.name: Matthew Meyer's Aka Manto entry
documentary.description: English-language documentation of the Aka Manto legend, including its 1930s origin and Osaka tradition.
documentary.source: Meyer, Matthew, yokai.com / The Hour of Meeting Evil Spirits

documentary.name: Atlas Obscura article
documentary.description: Eric Grundhauser, 'Aka Manto Is the Bathroom Ghost That Wants You to Choose Wisely', Atlas Obscura.

paranormal.name: Vengeful spirit of a murdered handsome man
paranormal.description: Some folk versions say Aka Manto was once a handsome young man whose face had to be hidden; in death he persists as a vengeful onryō who appears in lavatories.
evidence_cited: Reports of unearthly attractiveness beneath the mask

skeptical.name: Schoolyard urban legend / moral tale
skeptical.description: Folklorists treat Aka Manto as a classic urban legend transmitted through Japanese schools, functioning as a rite-of-passage scare and a way of negotiating anxieties around modern public bathrooms.
evidence_cited: Choice-based death structure typical of urban legends

skeptical.name: Echo of Showa-era 'red cloak' criminal scares
skeptical.description: Some Japanese commentators link Aka Manto to recurring early-Showa newspaper scares about a red-cloaked stranger preying on children, which then merged with bathroom-ghost folklore.
proponents: Japanese folklore commentators cited via Wikipedia

traditions: Bathroom-spirit folklore (alongside Hanako-san and the Akaname)
stories: Standard Aka Manto encounter: 'red paper or blue paper?' choice
Kainade variant (a coloured hairy arm reaches up from inside the toilet)
folklore.beliefs: Aka Manto is treated as a hostile spirit specifically tied to public and school toilets; standard 'protective' responses involve refusing both options or saying nothing.

literature: Bathroom Readers' Institute — Uncle John's OLD FAITHFUL 30th Anniversary Bathroom Reader (2017)
